results.markdown:
Title: Click-through rate by industry: dated benchmarks

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/click-through-rate-by-industry

Published Time: 2026-11-11T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
US search ads get clicked far more often than social or display ads. WordStream and LocaliQ’s 2026 benchmark puts the median click-through rate for US search ads on Google and Microsoft at 6.64%, measured April 2025 to March 2026.

Focus Digital’s 2026 study averages 0.90% on Facebook and 0.68% on Instagram, and its display study averages 0.46%.

## What click-through rate measures

Click-through rate (CTR) is the share of ad impressions that end in a click: clicks divided by impressions, times 100. An ad shown 1,000 times that gets 10 clicks has a 1% CTR. The formula is the same for search ads, social ads, display banners and email.

CTR counts direct clicks only. As [Choozle’s guide to click-through rate](https://choozle.com/blog/what-is-click-through-rate/) explains, someone who sees an ad, leaves, and later reaches the website another way doesn’t count toward CTR, even if the ad brought them there. Keep this in mind for every benchmark below. CTR tells you how often an ad pulled an immediate click. It doesn’t tell you how much business the ad produced.

The most widely used search benchmark is the annual report from WordStream and LocaliQ. Its 2026 edition covers US search campaigns on Google Ads and Microsoft Ads combined, from April 2025 to March 2026, and was published May 18, 2026. It puts the median CTR across all industries at 6.64%, according to the [WordStream 2026 Google Ads benchmarks](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/2026-google-ads-benchmarks), close to the 6.66% in the 2025 edition noted in [Digital Applied’s summary](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/google-ads-benchmarks-2026-cpc-ctr-cvr-industry).

![Image 1: Woman on a couch searching on her phone in a warmly lit living room](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/fd1d05702c7833b2a243c603ba08795b004bb616725e8af44a8da32e1403953b.jpg)

These figures are medians, not averages. They describe US accounts only, and they blend Google and Microsoft search, so they don’t describe either platform alone. The report covers many industries. The table shows the four whose figures we could confirm, as summarized by [Digital Applied’s breakdown of the 2026 edition](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/google-ads-benchmarks-2026-cpc-ctr-cvr-industry):

| Industry (US search, 2026 edition) | Median CTR | Median CPC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arts & Entertainment | 12.75% | $1.63 |
| Animals & Pets | 7.49% | $4.06 |
| Apparel / Fashion & Jewelry | 6.64% | $4.44 |
| Attorneys & Legal Services | 5.87% | $9.87 |
| All industries | 6.64% | $5.42 |

The spread is wide. Arts and entertainment searches, such as someone looking up showtimes or tickets, get clicked nearly twice as often as the cross-industry median and cost far less per click. Legal searches get clicked less often and cost much more. If you run a theater, a music hall or another venue, the guide to [campaigns for entertainment venues](https://adwave.com/industries/events-entertainment/entertainment-venues/tv-advertising-entertainment-venues) covers how search fits alongside other channels.

The CPC column is here only for context. Cost per click by industry has its own variation and caveats.

Social ads click at a fraction of the search rate, because people scrolling a feed aren’t looking for anything in particular. [Focus Digital’s 2026 social media ads study](https://focus-digital.co/social-media-ads-ctr-benchmarks-2025/) gives these averages across all campaign objectives:

| Platform | Average CTR, all objectives |
| --- | --- |
| Facebook | 0.90% |
| X | 0.86% |
| Instagram | 0.68% |
| TikTok | 0.61% |
| LinkedIn | 0.52% |

The campaign objective changes the figure a lot. In the same study, Facebook traffic campaigns average 1.93% and lead campaigns 2.70%. Those campaigns are optimized to find people likely to click, so judge a lead campaign against the lead figure, not the all-objective average.

The method shapes how far you can trust the finer splits. Focus Digital compiled published advertising benchmarks from August 2025 to October 2026, then used its own modeling to align time periods and fill gaps. Its industry figures for Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn and X are calculated from Facebook’s industry CTR and scaled by each platform’s average. They are estimates rather than measured results, so we don’t publish those splits here. The platform averages and the Facebook objective figures are the firmer numbers.

Display ads, the banners and image ads that run on websites and apps, get clicked least of the three. [Focus Digital’s display study](https://focus-digital.co/average-display-ad-ctr-2025-benchmarks/), covering February to December 2025, puts the average CTR at 0.46%. Real estate had the highest rate at 1.08%, which the study attributes to people actively researching property. B2B services had the lowest at 0.22%. Agents weighing display against other channels can see more in our guide to [advertising for real estate agents](https://adwave.com/industries/real-estate/real-estate-agents/tv-advertising-real-estate-agents).

Be careful with the 0.46% figure. The same number appears in [WordStream data from August 2017 to January 2018](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/display-advertising-benchmarks-2026-data-points), drawn from US client accounts across search and display, and it has been repeated on many pages since. A 2025 study landing on exactly the same rate may reflect stable behavior, or it may reflect sources quoting each other. Use 0.46% as a rough guide for display, not as a precise current measurement.

## Why CTV and TV are not judged by click-through rate

Viewers can’t click a TV screen, so connected TV (CTV) and broadcast ads have no real CTR to measure. Choozle’s guide says CTR shouldn’t be used alone to measure awareness channels such as video, CTV, audio and display. It suggests judging them on reach, frequency, viewability, video completion rate, site activity and conversions.

![Image 2: Family watching a large television in a dim living room at night](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/424aa84a4c0d65a1004c05f4e52f433b3f5eb5024bf97f5b3ed9eae077c16e92.jpg)

Search and retargeting capture demand that already exists, while CTV and digital audio create it. In a [Viant post on CTR](https://www.viantinc.com/insights/blog/why-ctr-is-misleading-in-digital-advertising/), Steven Ohrnstein, Viant’s SVP of Platform Automation & Analytics, describes channels like CTV and digital audio as ones that “create demand”. A TV spot might lead someone to search for your business days later, and that search ad then gets the click.

For TV, the metrics that matter are whether the ad was watched in full, how many households saw it and how often, and what happened on your website afterward. Our guide explains [how view-through rate works](https://adwave.com/resources/view-through-rate) for local businesses. For context on the channel itself, see [how fast CTV advertising is growing](https://adwave.com/resources/ctv-advertising-growth-rate).

## What a good CTR looks like for a local business

Compare like with like. A 1% CTR is weak for a search ad, about average for a Facebook ad across objectives, and well above average for a display banner. Use the benchmark for your channel, your campaign objective and, where one exists, your industry. A good CTR beats that figure and still brings in leads. Then track your own CTR over time, since your past results show what a change in creative or targeting actually did.

![Image 3: Bakery owner at the shop counter reviewing notes in morning light](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/41c926be29a12b476e1f397561f2f15a3bb8f808a5db46500a1102ad1cb7844c.jpg)

A high CTR isn’t the goal on its own. Viant’s Ohrnstein notes that a high CTR doesn’t always bring high-quality customers: an ad that pulls lots of curious, low-intent clicks can cost more per lead than one with fewer, better clicks. For a plumber, a dentist or a restaurant, the questions that matter are whether those clicks turned into calls, bookings or form fills, and what each one cost. Don’t rank channels by CTR either. A TV spot and a search ad do different jobs, and putting their click rates side by side hides that. Home service businesses can see how channels work together in our guide to [advertising for home service businesses](https://adwave.com/industries/home-services/remodeling/tv-advertising-home-services).

This is easier to judge when every channel reports in one place. Adwave creates ads from your website and runs them on TV, search, social and the web from one daily budget, starting at [$30 per day](https://adwave.com/pricing/). Channel availability depends on budget: TikTok, for example, starts from $91 per day and must be turned on. Adwave tracks campaign activity and [websit

results.title: Conversion rate by industry: 2026 benchmarks
results.markdown:
Title: Conversion rate by industry: 2026 benchmarks

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/conversion-rate-by-industry

Published Time: 2026-11-10T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Insights

## Average ad conversion rate by industry in 2026

Dated conversion rate benchmarks by industry and channel from named sources, what each one counts as a conversion, and how to compare your own rate.

![Image 1: Conversion rate by industry: 2026 benchmarks](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/9fb95a5b768622f4010deb1542e71ee1b80087555e8124daa7eefb21741d5ecb.jpg)

There is no single conversion rate by industry that applies to every business. WordStream/LocaliQ’s 2026 benchmark puts the median US search ad conversion rate at 8.18%, ranging from 2.64% in finance and insurance to 16.22% in animals and pets.

Site-wide and ecommerce benchmarks run lower, around 2% to 8%, because they divide by sessions or visitors instead of ad clicks.

## What a conversion rate measures and why benchmarks disagree

A conversion rate is the number of conversions divided by the number of chances to convert, multiplied by 100. The formula is simple. Sources disagree because they choose different things to divide by and different things to count. The denominator can be ad clicks, sessions or unique visitors. The conversion can be a completed purchase, a form submission, a phone call, or any action an advertiser chooses to track.

![Image 2: Two marketers at a desk comparing notes with a calculator in a small sunlit office](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/cac7e9ae1f9be4b65a6b5f6010e24e20591e357f9baf5eecb971bc4334bcb23a.jpg)

The same week of paid search traffic can produce three different rates. For example, Google Ads might credit 120 purchases to 2,000 clicks, which is 6.0%, and that count can include buyers who came back days later on another device. Google Analytics might count 60 sessions with a purchase out of 2,500 paid search sessions, which is 2.4%. The store’s order system might match 57 orders to 3,000 sessions it tagged as paid search, which is 1.9%. Each number is correct for its own definition.

Session-based rates have a further quirk. When buyers make several visits before they convert, the session rate falls even though the same share of people end up buying. A business with a long consideration cycle can look worse on a session benchmark than it really is. The tables below therefore can’t be ranked against each other. Use each one only alongside a rate of your own that is defined the same way.

The largest recent paid search benchmark comes from WordStream and LocaliQ. Their 2026 search ad benchmarks found a median conversion rate of 8.18% across 13,474 US campaigns on Google Ads and Microsoft Ads between April 2025 and March 2026, [as summarized in Digital Applied’s landing page statistics](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/landing-page-statistics-2026-conversion-data-points). The rate is conversions per ad click. It counts every conversion action advertisers track, so a form fill, a call and a purchase all count the same. Industry rates in that dataset run from 2.64% in finance and insurance to 16.22% in animals and pets. WordStream calls these medians “averages,” [a definitional note recorded by Digital Applied](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/conversion-rate-benchmarks-2026-industry-channel). WordStream publishes the full industry charts on its [Google Ads benchmarks 2026 page](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/2026-google-ads-benchmarks), which was last updated September 16, 2026.

The series has moved over time. WordStream’s first report, in 2016, gave 2.70%. Its 2025 report gave 7.52%, according to [WordStream’s Google Ads performance study](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/google-ads-performance). That same study notes that accounts run through its Google Ads Grader convert below the benchmark, which is drawn from accounts on the LocaliQ platform. Treat 8.18% as a figure from managed accounts, not as a floor every account should clear. A low rate in a regulated, high-consideration category is normal. Our guide to [advertising for financial advisors](https://adwave.com/industries/financial/financial-advisory/tv-advertising-financial-advisors) covers how to plan around longer decision cycles.

## Website conversion rate by industry across all traffic

Ruler Analytics’ [conversion rate benchmark study](https://www.ruleranalytics.com/blog/insight/conversion-rate-by-industry/), published May 26, 2026, covers 13 industries, more than 110 million sessions and more than 5 million tracked conversions. It counts form submissions and phone calls as conversions, across all traffic sources rather than ads alone.

| Industry | Average conversion rate |
| --- | --- |
| Automotive | 7.9% |
| Legal | 7.9% |
| Software | 7.6% |
| Education | 6.3% |
| Finance | 6.3% |
| Marketing & Advertising | 6.2% |
| Professional Services | 6.1% |
| Construction & Engineering | 4.9% |
| Beauty & Cosmetic | 3.5% |
| Real Estate | 2.8% |
| Retail & eCommerce | 2.4% |
| Health & Social Care | 2.3% |
| Travel | 1.9% |

Ruler reports the spend it tracked in pounds (£33.8M+). Our reading is that the sample probably leans toward UK businesses, so US advertisers should treat it as directional. Because calls count as conversions, phone-heavy categories score well here. If you run [advertising for auto dealerships](https://adwave.com/industries/automotive/auto-dealerships/tv-advertising-auto-dealerships), make sure your own tracking counts calls before you compare against that 7.9%. Real estate’s 2.8% reflects how long buyers browse listings before they make contact, which matters when you plan [ads for real estate agents](https://adwave.com/industries/real-estate/real-estate-agents/tv-advertising-real-estate-agents).

## Conversion rates by channel and industry

Ruler also splits its data by traffic source. Its paid search rates by industry are below.

![Image 3: Person on a sofa holding a phone with a laptop and a lit television nearby in the evening](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/2c48447ba777e74d63c4e7bd4621c1b772709860d2ac4db75ad8b55760fa3e14.jpg)

| Industry | Paid search conversion rate |
| --- | --- |
| Marketing & Advertising | 8.9% |
| Automotive | 8.6% |
| Software | 8.2% |
| Legal | 7.8% |
| Professional Services | 6.7% |
| Finance | 6.3% |
| Education | 5.7% |
| Construction & Engineering | 5.1% |
| Beauty & Cosmetic | 4.2% |
| Real Estate | 3.7% |
| Travel | 2.2% |
| Retail & eCommerce | 2.1% |
| Health & Social Care | 1.2% |

Across all industries, Ruler found AI referral traffic converting at 5.8%, email at 4.9%, organic social at 2.23% and paid social at 2.11%. Ruler describes the AI referral figure as early data from modest volumes.

These paid search rates sit below WordStream’s 8.18% median because the two studies measure different things. Ruler divides by sessions and counts forms and calls. WordStream divides by ad clicks and counts every tracked action. Neither figure is wrong. In our view, TV and streaming ads fit poorly with a per-click rate, so it makes sense to judge them on other measures. If you plan [campaigns for home service businesses](https://adwave.com/industries/home-services/remodeling/tv-advertising-home-services) that mix TV with search, judge each channel on the measure that fits it.

## Ecommerce conversion rates by industry

Purchase-based benchmarks count completed orders. They come out lower than lead-based rates, and each one uses a different period and scope:

*   **Dynamic Yield:** 2.68% average ecommerce conversion rate (completed purchases per visitor) across 400+ brands, October 2025 to September 2026. By industry, beauty and personal care reached 5.38%, food and beverage 4.56%, and fashion, accessories and apparel 2.74%. These figures come from [Digital Applied’s 2026 benchmark roundup](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/conversion-rate-benchmarks-2026-industry-channel). A separate reading of Dynamic Yield’s rolling 12-month benchmark, [reported by Blend Commerce](https://blendcommerce.com/blogs/shopify/ecommerce-conversion-rate-benchmarks-2026?srsltid=AYCX9vI9eFNaooUJCTQFwvg1t34Rjz2ODhzfoMDiQHlS6jievk6h0uf8), showed a 2.72% global average.
*   **Contentsquare:** 2.3% of visits included a conversion event (a purchase or form submission) across 6,500+ websites in Q4 2025.
*   **IRP Commerce:** 1.97% of sessions ended in a transaction for UK and Irish merchants in September 2026, up from 1.68% in September 2025. Blend Commerce also reports an IRP reading of 2.26% for July 2026.
*   **Littledata:** 1.4% of sessions included a purchase at the median Shopify store, July to October 2026, across 433 stores.

The gap between these figures comes mostly from the denominator. Rates per visitor run above rates per session. A considered purchase pulls the rate down further, which is why a retailer running [advertising for jewelry stores](https://adwave.com/industries/retail/jewelr

results.title: Google Ads Benchmarks for YOUR Industry [Updated!]
results.markdown:
Title: Google Ads Benchmarks for YOUR Industry [Updated!]

URL Source: https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2016/02/29/google-adwords-industry-benchmarks

Published Time: 2016-02-19T05:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Whether you’re doing PPC for the first time or you’ve just signed a new client, it can be daunting to know whether or not you’re doing a good job. Sure, we all want to create unicorn ads that have [highest CTRs](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2014/02/11/average-click-through-rate) and the [best conversion rates](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2014/03/17/what-is-a-good-conversion-rate), but what’s a good metric for one industry isn’t necessarily good for another. So what numbers should you be looking to beat in your industry?

Check out the Google Ads industry benchmarks our clients are seeing, including:

*   Average click-through rate (CTR)
*   Average cost per click (CPC)
*   Average conversion rate (CVR)
*   Average cost per action (CPA)

You’ll find averages across these ads metrics for twenty industries: Advocacy, Auto, B2B, Consumer Services, Dating & Personals, E-Commerce, Education, Employment Services, Finance & Insurance, Health & Medical, Home Goods, Industrial Services, Legal, Real Estate, Technology, and Travel & Hospitality.

**![Image 1: ✴️](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/2734.svg) Note:**We update this data regularly! **[Download the PDF of our latest Google Ads Benchmarks report here](https://www.wordstream.com/resources/google-ads-industry-benchmarks?cid=Web_WS_InContent_Guide_GoogleAdsBenchmarks_Download&itm_source=wordstream&itm_medium=blog&itm_campaign=incontent_links).**

## Average Click-Through Rate in Google Ads by Industry

![Image 2: average ctr in adwords](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/adwords-industry-benchmarks-average-ctr-3.png)

Dating and personal services really _click_ with PPC – boasting an average search CTR of 6%! No doubt, it’s easy to [write powerful emotional ad copy](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2015/11/09/emotional-ads) when your prospects are searching for love. Other industries with high search CTRs include Advocacy, Autos, and Travel.

When we first collected this data in 2015, legal services could struggle to attract attention on the SERP (with a relatively low average 1.35% CTR) – in large part due to [advertising restrictions](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2014/11/25/adwords-ad-disapproved) enforced by both Google and government organizations. [Legal advertisers](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2015/06/29/law-firm-marketing) have improved their stats in the past few years!

As of 2018, the industries with the lowest average click-through rates including Technology, B2B, and Consumer Services.

**The average click-through rate in Google Ads across all industries is 3.17% for search and 0.46% for display.**

Both of these averages are higher than they were a couple of years ago: Good news for Ads advertisers and agencies!

### Average Click Through Rate (CTR)

| Industry | Average CTR (Search) | Average CTR (GDN) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Advocacy | 4.41% | 0.59% |
| Auto | 4.00% | 0.60% |
| B2B | 2.41% | 0.46% |
| Consumer Services | 2.41% | 0.51% |
| Dating & Personals | 6.05% | 0.72% |
| E-Commerce | 2.69% | 0.51% |
| Education | 3.78% | 0.53% |
| Employment Services | 2.42% | 0.59% |
| Finance & Insurance | 2.91% | 0.52% |
| Health & Medical | 3.27% | 0.59% |
| Home Goods | 2.44% | 0.49% |
| Industrial Services | 2.61% | 0.50% |
| Legal | 2.93% | 0.59% |
| Real Estate | 3.71% | 1.08% |
| Technology | 2.09% | 0.39% |
| Travel & Hospitality | 4.68% | 0.47% |

![Image 3: 📙](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/1f4d9.svg)**Free guide [>> Hacking Google Ads: One Trick That Could Save You Thousands](https://marketing.wordstream.com/WSLIQContentDLWebsiteHackingGoogleAds.html?cid=Web_Any_BlogInContent_PPC_HackingGoogleAds_Download)**

## Average Cost Per Click in Google Ads by Industry

![Image 4: contextual display costs](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/adwords-industry-benchmarks-average-cpc-5.png)

It’s no surprise that legal services have some of the highest CPCs among all Google ads on the search network. Both “Lawyer” and “Attorney” make the top 10 [most expensive keywords on Google](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2011/07/18/most-expensive-keywords-google-adwords) and [on Bing](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2015/03/19/most-expensive-keywords-bing-ads). Average CPCs in the legal industry are over $6. Consumer services aren’t too far behind, with an average CPC of $6.40.

Advocacy and nonprofit groups are fortunate to have a cost per click under $2, likely as a result of the $2 max CPC bid [Google Grant advertisers](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2013/12/18/google-grants-adwords-for-nonprofits) have to set on all of their [keywords](https://www.wordstream.com/keywords).

Most industries have pretty inexpensive CPCs on the Google Display Network. The only industry with costs per click over $1 on the Display network is Dating & Personals.

**The average cost per click in Google Ads across all industries is $2.69 for search and $0.63 for display.**

The news here is good too: These [Google Ads costs](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2015/05/21/how-much-does-adwords-cost) have increased very little over the figures we found a couple of years ago (when the averages were $2.32 and $0.58 respectively).

### Average Cost Per Click (CPC)

| Industry | Average CPC (Search) | Average CPC (GDN) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Advocacy | $1.43 | $0.62 |
| Auto | $2.46 | $0.58 |
| B2B | $3.33 | $0.79 |
| Consumer Services | $6.40 | $0.81 |
| Dating & Personals | $2.78 | $1.49 |
| E-Commerce | $1.16 | $0.45 |
| Education | $2.40 | $0.47 |
| Employment Services | $2.04 | $0.78 |
| Finance & Insurance | $3.44 | $0.86 |
| Health & Medical | $2.62 | $0.63 |
| Home Goods | $2.94 | $0.60 |
| Industrial Services | $2.56 | $0.54 |
| Legal | $6.75 | $0.72 |
| Real Estate | $2.37 | $0.75 |
| Technology | $3.80 | $0.51 |
| Travel & Hospitality | $1.53 | $0.44 |

## Average Conversion Rates in Google Ads by Industry

![Image 5: average conversion rate in adwords](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/adwords-industry-benchmarks-average-conversion-rate-2.png)

A couple of years ago, the Finance and Insurance industries were leading the pack when it came to conversion rates.

However, our newly updated data shows that the Dating & Personal industry is way out ahead now, with search conversion rates on average over 9%! Other standouts include the legal industries, consumer services, and autos.

In many of these cases, the best converting advertisers aren’t afraid to change their offer or their conversion flow to boost their conversion rates. Or they may be taking advantage of conversion-boosting tactics such as video landing pages.

[Ecommerce clients](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2019/04/01/shopping-ads-benchmarks) may not have many options to change their offer and consequently suffer one of the poorer average conversion rates on both search and display. To boot, they often have gigantic inventories, which prevents doing fine-tuning on ad copy across all [ecommerce keywords](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2016/01/21/e-commerce-keyword-research).

Brought to you by

![Image 6: wordstream logo](https://www.wordstream.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/WS-Logo-2023.webp)

## Ready to grow your business?

Unlock the results you’re looking for with technology-backed solutions designed for small businesses and agencies.

While removing barriers to purchase will always be an important CRO tool to help ecommerce clients, Google Ads advertisers should focus on improving the performance of their [keywords with high commercial intent](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/ws/2014/06/30/commercial-intent-keywords) to yield the most out of their search campaigns.

**The average conversion rate in google ads across all industries is 3.75% for search and 0.77% for display.**

Since the last time we compiled this data, search conversion rates have risen slightly, but display conversion rates have fallen slightly, perhaps a sign that display advertisers need to pay more attention to placements and audience optimization.

### Average Conversion Rate (CVR)

| Industry | Average CVR (Search) | Average CVR (GDN) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Advocacy | 1.96% | 1.00% |
| Auto | 6.03% | 1.19% |
| B2B | 3.04% | 0.80% |
| Consumer Services | 6.64% | 0.98% |
| Dating & Personals | 9.64% | 3.34% |
| E-Commerce | 2.81% | 0.59% |
| Education | 3.39% | 0.50% |
| Employment Services | 5.13% | 1.57% |
| Finance & Insurance | 5.10% | 1.19% |
| Health & Medical | 3.36% | 0.82% |
| Home Goods | 2.70% | 0.43% |
| Industrial Services | 3.37% | 0.94% |
| Legal | 6.98% | 1.84% |
| Real Estate | 2.47% | 0.80% |
| Technology | 2.92% | 0.86% |
| Travel & Hospitality | 3.55% | 0.51% |

results.title: NEW 2026 Search Advertising Benchmarks (+Tips)
results.markdown:
Title: NEW 2026 Search Advertising Benchmarks (+Tips)

URL Source: https://localiq.com/blog/search-advertising-benchmarks/

Published Time: 2026-05-26T12:30:08+00:00

Markdown Content:
As a business owner, you want to capture searchers and turn them into customers—especially when [88%](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/consumer-insights/consumer-trends/local-search-to-store-visit-statistics/) of searches for a local business result in a call or visit.

It makes search advertising a no-brainer. But I’ve spent enough time staring at account reports to know how difficult it can be to predict the average campaign performance. For instance, what’s the average click-through rate, cost per click, or conversion rate for search ads? Are your results in line with industry averages? What can be done to improve your search advertising results if not?

In partnership with WordStream by LocaliQ, we’ve dug into the data from thousands of our customers’ advertising campaigns across Google Ads and Microsoft Ads to create [search advertising benchmarks](https://www.wordstream.com/blog/2026-google-ads-benchmarks) for the top 20+ industries.

![Image 1: google ads benchmarks averages](https://localiq.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Averages.webp)

I’m sharing some of the data along with expert insights and tips here. But if you want **to check out the full charts and comparisons (which I highly recommend!), download the full report >>**[2026 Search Advertising Benchmarks for Your Industry](https://localiq.com/resources/search-advertising-benchmarks-report/?cid=Web_LiQ_Any_InContent_Guide_GoogleAdsBenchmarks_Download&itm_source=localiq&itm_medium=blog&itm_campaign=incontent_links).

### Contents

*   [Expert tips to improve your search campaigns](https://localiq.com/blog/search-advertising-benchmarks/#search-ads-tips)

## Average cost per click for search advertising

Search advertising is a cost-effective advertising strategy—and the average cost per click (CPC) really shows that across all industries we looked at, despite a bit of an increase over the last year.

**The average CPC for search advertising across all industries in 2026 is $5.42.**

The lowest average cost per click came from Arts and Entertainment at $1.63, while Restaurants and Food was close behind at only $2.05 per click.

A few other industries, including Travel and Sports & Recreation, had relatively low CPCs under $3.

Cliff Sizemore, Senior Marketing Manager at LocaliQ, said CPC is a metric he generally keeps a close eye on, but not without factoring in other metrics as well.

“Focusing too much on cost per click can lead you to cheaper clicks that don’t convert. I pay close attention to conversion rate and cost per lead in relation to CPC,” he said.

## Average click-through rate for search advertising

In search advertising, your click-through rate (CTR) can tell you a lot. A low CTR might be a sign of a poor offer, insufficient targeting, or ad copy in need of optimization.

High CTR would tell you that your search ads are connecting with your audience—and driving them to take action.

**The average CTR for search advertising in 2026 across industries is 6.64%.**

Every expert we talked to agreed that CTR is a great indicator of how your search advertising campaigns are performing.

“CTR tells you how your ads are performing and can provide valuable information you can use to optimize your search ads to pull in more clicks—and more conversions,” said Susie Marino, PPC expert and LocaliQ senior content marketing specialist.

Amy Bishop, Senior Vice President of Performance Marketing at Waystar, said that while CTR is a good metric to measure, it shouldn’t be the main indicator of PPC success.

“I generally advise that CPC and CTR are health metrics. They’re important to keep a pulse on and to use as levers to achieve your goals. However, they aren’t KPIs. Focusing too much on CPCs or CTR as a KPI can be detrimental, so it’s important that bettering these metrics is never at the expense of more important metrics like return on advertising spend,” she said.

## Average cost per lead for search advertising

Cost per lead (CPL) is an essential PPC metric for your search advertising campaigns. It measures more than just an action taken on your ad—it shows how much you spend for a user to click on your ad and contact you in some way, whether by phone, chat, form fill, or email.

## Email Marketing Benchmarks and Metrics Businesses Should Track

Wondering how your email marketing metrics compare to others in your industry? Check out these email marketing benchmarks to understand how you’re doing.

## Nice work!

## Email marketing benchmarks play a pivotal role in providing businesses with a comprehensive understanding of their campaign performance and industry standards.

These benchmarks serve as vital metrics that enable businesses to gauge the effectiveness of their email marketing strategy.

By comparing key performance indicators (KPIs) such as open rates, click-through rates, and conversion rates against industry averages, businesses can identify areas of strength and weakness in their campaigns while measuring their performance against competitors and industry leaders.

In assessing and optimizing marketing performance, email marketing benchmarks can act as a compass for businesses, guiding them toward data-driven decision-making. By tracking metrics and marketing benchmarks, companies can fine-tune their email marketing strategies to help enhance engagement and retention.

Email marketing benchmarks can provide a baseline against which businesses can set targets for improvements and measure the success of their optimization efforts. Additionally, they offer a framework for testing and experimenting with different elements of email campaigns, such as subject lines, visuals, and call-to-action buttons.

Meanwhile, finding an industry average for each important business metric can further enhance this process by offering context and insights tailored to the unique dynamics and expectations of particular sectors, empowering businesses to make informed, strategic designs that align with their goals.

Keep reading to find our email marketing campaign stats by industry to help benchmark your email marketing performance.

## Average email marketing campaign statistics by industry

There are a lot of numbers in Mailchimp’s reports on email and marketing automation, but you might be wondering how your stats compare to others in the same industry. What kind of open rates should companies like yours expect? How many bounces are too many? What's the average click-through rate for businesses like yours? What data do content marketers rely upon to improve engagement rates? The more context, the better.

Mailchimp sends billions of emails a month for millions of users. Needless to say, we track a lot of data. So we scanned billions of emails delivered by our system (where campaign tracking was activated, and where users reported their industry) and calculated the average unique open rates, click rates, soft bounce rate, and hard bounce rate by industry.

We only tracked campaigns that went to at least 1,000 subscribers. Our customers range from 1-person startups, small businesses to Fortune 500 companies, so the whole spectrum is represented in this data. Here’s your apples-to-apples comparison of email marketing metrics with others in your industry.

The data provided on this page was last updated in December 2023 and may vary from email marketing benchmarks data provided within the Mailchimp application.

*Disclaimers

The accuracy of email open rates may be impacted by Apple's privacy changes and their Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) feature, and this should be considered as you interpret open rate data.

These figures are based on available data as of December 2023 By leveraging our extensive data analysis on email and marketing automation, businesses can gain invaluable insights into industry-specific benchmarks, offering a deeper understanding of their campaign performance. Companies can now contextualize their own metrics by examining open rates, click-through rates, and bounce rates.

Armed with the knowledge of industry performance, companies can establish realistic objectives and tailor their strategies for optimal engagement. Whether fine-turning content for better click-through rates or addressing bounce rates, these benchmarks provide a baseline for improvement.

## Strategies for improving open rates

Achieving higher open rates in email marketing can be a fundamental goal for businesses aiming to enhance their reach and engagement with their audience. The open rate measures the percentage of recipients who open an email and is a KPI that can reflect the effectiveness of your email campaigns.

Let’s dive into a few of the best strategies for helping improve open rates:

### 1. Craft compelling subject lines to boost email open rates

Subject lines are the gateway to your email content, making them a critical component of any email marketing campaign. They’re the first impression your audience has of your email, and can influence their decision to open or ignore your message.

A well-crafted subject line can pique curiosity, convey value, and establish a connection with your subscribers.

Let’s explore some of the best practices to help guide you in crafting compelling subject lines that entice your audience and elevate your email marketing campaigns:

**Personalized email subject lines**

Use merge tags to personalize your subject lines with each recipient's name or location. Personalized emails may increase open rates for most users, and may work well when combined with marketing automation in transactional emails, such as birthday deals, post-purchase follow-ups or promotional emails.

**Be descriptive**

Sometimes, it's better to be direct and descriptive than trendy. Seasonal slogans such as "Fall into savings" or "Sizzling summer bargains" are popular but don't offer a specific hook. Instead, try to communicate the benefits of your promotions, or call attention to specific deals.

**Keep it short**

For many recipients, especially those reading your emails on mobile devices, shorter is often better. We recommend you use no more than 9 words and 60 characters.

**Limit punctuation**

Our research shows that it’s best to use no more than 3 punctuation marks per subject line. Too many punctuation marks can make your email look like spam, especially if you use a lot of special characters.

**Use emojis carefully**

Our built-in emoji picker is a fun and easy way to add some visual pizazz to your subject lines. However, there are a few things to keep in mind when you use emojis.

According to our research, you should use no more than 1 emoji at a time. Use emojis to supplement words rather than replace them, to make sure your main message gets across. Different operating systems render different versions of emojis, so it’s important to test.

### 2. Optimize audience segmentation for enhanced open rates

Audience segmentation is a cornerstone of successful email marketing. Rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all approach, segmentation involves categorizing your email subscribers based on specific criteria, such as demographics, behavior, or preferences.

By understanding the unique characteristics and needs of different segments within your audience, you can tailor your email content to be more relevant and personalized. This targeted approach can foster a stronger connection with subscribers and can significantly enhance the likelihood of capturing their attention and driving higher open rates.

Let’s take a look at a few tips for optimizing audience segmentation:

**Keep your segments more widely defined**

Although the point of audience segmentation is to aim for specificity, it’s possible to segment your audience too far. It’s essential to have a smaller market with a defined need. If your market is so narrowly defined that it barely contains anyone, however, that’s a problem. You’ll either reach too few people, or you’ll end up spending time and energy writing messages for too many different audiences. Focus on a few groups, but keep those groups broad enough to encompass relatively wide swaths of your customer base.

**Aim for constant improvement**

If the combination of audience segmentation strategies you used didn’t work, experiment with another mix until you find the most effective way to reach your potential customers. Measure the data to see where people are landing on your site, how long they’re staying, and what’s making them leave. Then incorporate that data into your next effort and into the day-to-day operations of your marketing.
